<document>
# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
This is the most informative document in the set. It runs the tests the earlier papers called for:
- a registered mediation analysis,
- a second hours measure that doesn't depend on what staff claim,
- a randomised two-year horizon,
- an account of which studies sat behind the meta-analysis's long-follow-up subgroup.

It also settles two disputes. The four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, as I suspected, so the meta-analysis's "no decay" claim fails. And a gain of about 8–10% per actual hour persists at two years, so Varga and Holm's "entirely an artifact" claim fails too.

The arithmetic checks out:

| Figure | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Output per timesheet hour | 0.966 / 0.88 | +9.8% |
| Output per log hour | 0.966 / 0.89 | +8.5% |
| Halden continuers, output per hour | 96.8 / 86.6 | +11.8% |
| Halden continuers, hours change | 34.9 / 40.3 | −13.4% |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 | 100% |

The counter-arm costing is also internally consistent. With 12% more staff each working 17% fewer hours, total hours are 0.93 of baseline. At the 6.7% per-hour gain from the nine-month report, that restores roughly 99% of baseline output.

The main problems are below.

## 1. A contaminated control group partly explains the "decline"

In month 15, two of the seven control offices held a meeting audit and raised their output per hour by about 4%. That improves the control arm and shrinks the difference-in-differences estimate. A rough calculation: 2 of 7 offices × 4.1% ≈ 1.2 points of the 2.7-point fall from 12.5% to 9.8%. So up to about 40% of the apparent fading could be control offices improving, not treated offices regressing.

The paper presents the audit as supporting evidence for the meetings mechanism but never considers what it does to the main estimate. It should report two sensitivity analyses:
- the 24-month estimates excluding those two offices,
- the estimates truncated at month 15.

It's also likely that the audit was prompted by the trial itself. That is spillover to the control arm, which office-level randomisation was meant to prevent.

## 2. The Summary mixes hours measures

The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months". The 12.5% is per timesheet hour and the 8.5% is per log hour. On the same measure the decline is 12.5% → 9.8%, about a fifth, not a third. §5's "declined by about a quarter" is also somewhat generous.

The nine-month and 24-month confidence intervals overlap heavily, so "the gain has therefore declined" is stated more firmly than the data allow. "Consistent with some fading", the wording in §3, is the accurate version.

## 3. What do the system logs measure?

The paper calls log-in time the "stricter measure", yet two points need explaining:
- **Meetings.** If logs record only time working on cases, they exclude meetings. Treated offices cut meetings by about 3.3 hours relative to control, out of a timesheet fall of about 4.5 hours. Logged case time should then have fallen only a few percent, not 11%. Either logs include meeting time and idle logged-in sessions, or the figures don't reconcile. The paper should say what counts as "active" time.
- **Baseline.** Log hours appear only at 24 months. Was there pre-period log data for the difference-in-differences calculation, or was this measure added when the follow-up protocol was filed at month 11?

## 4. The mediation analysis: a real advance, but "confirms" is too strong

**What it does well.** Registering the mediation test before the outcomes were known is exactly the right response to the criticism that the meetings finding was post hoc.

**Why "confirms" is too strong:**
- **Assumptions.** Mediation relies on there being no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome. The Limitations section says so, but the Summary still says "confirms". Managers who cut meetings probably made other changes too, so the 47% may also pick up those changes.
- **Effective sample size.** The analysis has many "office-months", but office-months within an office aren't independent. The effective sample is still 14 offices, and the problem of too few clusters I raised at nine months still applies. An interval of 28–66% looks narrow for 14 clusters.
- **Partly accounting.** With timesheet hours as the denominator, cutting meetings mechanically raises cases per hour if time spent on cases holds steady. That *is* the "removing low-value time" hypothesis, so it isn't a confound. But it means this pathway reflects how hours are counted, not people working harder, and the paper could say so plainly.
- **Displacement.** Calendar data covers recurring meetings only. Some may have been replaced by ad hoc ones.

The unplanned meeting audit adds to this evidence. A 2.1-hour cut producing about 4% is roughly the size the mediation estimate would predict. It is still two offices, uncontrolled, and the paper rightly treats it that way.

## 5. The Halden follow-up has selection on top of selection

- **Non-response.** Only 14 of the 23 organisations with records responded. Organisations that reverted or did poorly are probably less likely to reply.
- **Survivorship.** The paper is admirably candid that the 11 continuers are survivors twice over.
- **Baseline hours.** The baseline of 40.3 hours is identical to the baseline Varga and Holm reported for the 27-organisation time-tracking group, while their 17-organisation subset had 40.4. An 11-organisation subset could match exactly, but it's worth confirming the right baseline was used.
- **Reversion pattern.** One reverting organisation is a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Work coded as "discretionary" can still be tied to clients' timing, which supports the meta-analysis's own caveat that the work-type classification is too coarse.

## 6. Items requested at nine months, still missing

- **Backlog and time-to-decision.** The nine-month report listed backlogs breaching statutory deadlines as a risk. Two years in, this should be measurable.
- **Cost per case.** Output per employee has drifted from −2.1% to −3.4%, at full pay plus overtime. The county costed the counter arm but not case processing.
- **Uncertainty on secondary outcomes.** Appeal overturn rates and resignations still have no confidence intervals or pre-period values.
- **Small-cluster inference.** Methods suited to so few clusters, such as wild cluster bootstrap or randomisation inference, still aren't used.

## 7. Authorship and correcting the record

Okafor co-authors a paper that judges critiques of his own pilot, and the Varden authors judge critiques of their own hypothesis. §5 is mostly fair: it concedes the re-analysis was right about measurement. The phrase "since dismissed as post hoc", however, reads as vindication.

More importantly, with a Halden author on board, this was the natural place to correct the working paper's description of attrition. Varga and Holm showed that seven of the nine dropouts left after the schedule began, mostly citing workload. The follow-up doesn't mention this.

## Bottom line

The central findings are well supported:
- In case-processing work, a randomised 20% cut in scheduled hours produced about an 11–12% cut in actual hours, a small loss of output per employee, and a per-hour gain of roughly 8–10% persisting at two years.
- Cutting meetings is plausibly the largest single contributor, with fatigue a smaller one.
- Coverage-bound work could not sustain the schedule without extra staff.

The revisions I'd ask for are:
1. Rerun the estimates without the contaminated control offices.
2. Compare like-for-like hours measures in the Summary.
3. Define the log-in measure and show its baseline.
4. Soften "confirms".
5. Add backlog and cost data.
6. Correct the record on Halden's attrition.

Across all five documents, the evidence now points to a modest, real per-hour gain in discretionary work, much of it from reorganisation that the hours cut forced. That gain does not cover the lost hours in coverage-bound work. The open policy question is the one the paper itself identifies: can the reorganisation be had without the hours cut? Only a trial arm that reorganises without reducing hours can answer it.

I can draft a referee report, or write up the five-document synthesis.
